forms.da: jeg går i biografen af og til
forms.en: I go to the cinema now and then

af og til.explanation: "Af og til" means now and then, or from time to time. It is a set phrase of three words and means about the same as "nogle gange" (sometimes). It is not as often as "ofte", but more often than "sjældent" (rarely). It is good in everyday talk: "Jeg cykler af og til".

sentence.da: Jeg ser min familie **af og til**.
sentence.en: I see my family now and then.

aflyst.explanation: "Aflyst" means cancelled, for example a train, a flight or an event that will not take place. You will see it on departure boards at stations and airports. It adds "-e" when you talk about more than one thing: "aflyste tog". It is a bit different from "forsinket", which only means delayed.

sentence.en: My flight is cancelled.

afrika.explanation: "Afrika" is the Danish name for Africa, and it is written with a capital letter. You say "i Afrika" for being there and "til Afrika" for going there. A person from Africa is "en afrikaner", and the describing word is "afrikansk". It is one of the seven continents, "verdensdele".

sentence.da: Han rejser til **Afrika** i næste måned.
sentence.en: He is travelling to Africa next month.

afsted.explanation: "Afsted" means off or away, and it is used about leaving for somewhere: "Vi skal afsted" means "We have to get going". You will also see it written as two words, "af sted". It often goes with "at tage" (to take) or "at komme" (to come).

sentence.en: We have to go now.

aftensmad.explanation: "Aftensmad" is dinner, the main meal of the day, eaten in the evening. It is built from "aften" (evening) and "mad" (food). Danes often eat it early, around six o'clock. A common phrase is "Hvad skal vi have til aftensmad?".

sentence.en: What are we having for dinner?

aldrig.explanation: "Aldrig" means never. In a main sentence it goes right after the verb: "Jeg drikker aldrig kaffe" (I never drink coffee). You do not need another "not" word, because "aldrig" already makes the sentence negative. The opposite is "altid" (always).

sentence.en: I never eat meat.

alene.explanation: "Alene" means alone or on your own. It stays the same no matter who is alone, so it never changes its ending. It describes being without other people, not necessarily lonely, and for the feeling of being lonely Danes say "ensom". "Helt alene" means all alone.

sentence.da: Jeg bor **alene** i en lille lejlighed.
sentence.en: I live alone in a small apartment.

alkohol.explanation: "Alkohol" is alcohol, and it is an en-word. It is the same idea as in English and is not counted. You will often see "alkoholfri" (alcohol-free) on drink menus, and "med alkohol" means with alcohol. Danes also say "en øl" for a beer and "en vin" for a wine.

sentence.en: Is there alcohol in that drink?

alle.explanation: "Alle" means "everyone" or "all" when you talk about people or many things: "Alle kan komme" (Everyone can come). "Alle sammen" means "all together" or "all of you". For "everything" use "alt", and for one single thing "hver".

sentence.en: Everyone in the class can swim.

allerede.explanation: "Allerede" means already. It is placed after the verb in a normal sentence: "Han er allerede her" (He is already here). It often shows that something happened sooner than expected. The matching word for the opposite is "endnu ikke" (not yet).

sentence.en: You are here already!

allergisk.explanation: "Allergisk" means allergic. To say what you are allergic to, use "over for": "Jeg er allergisk over for nødder". Pharmacies and doctors ask about this often, so it is a very useful word when you travel or visit the doctor.

sentence.en: I am allergic to nuts.

alt.explanation: "Alt" means "everything" or "all", as in "Alt er godt" (Everything is good). "Det er alt" means "That is all". It can also come before a describing word to mean "too" in some phrases, like "alt for dyrt" (far too expensive). For people, use "alle" instead.

sentence.en: She has forgotten everything.

altid.explanation: "Altid" means always. It usually goes right after the verb in a normal sentence: "Jeg er altid træt" (I am always tired). It is a very common word, and it is written as one word. The opposite is "aldrig" (never), and "ofte" is the milder word for often.

sentence.en: He always comes too late.

altså.explanation: "Altså" is a small word that can mean so, thus or well, and it is often used to sum up or to add emphasis. Danes use it a lot in speech: "Det er altså rigtigt!" means "It really is true!". Its exact meaning depends on the situation, so learn it from examples.

sentence.en: So you are not coming after all?

amerikansk.explanation: "Amerikansk" means American, for things from the USA. It has no capital letter in Danish. It stays "amerikansk" before an et-word and becomes "amerikanske" for more than one thing. The person is "en amerikaner". Danes often see "amerikanske film" and "amerikanske serier" on TV.

sentence.en: It is an American film.

anden.explanation: "Anden" means second, and it also means "other". With en-words you use "anden" ("min anden bil"), with et-words "andet" ("det andet hus"), and with plural words "andre". The context tells you whether it means second or other. For dates, "den anden juni" is the second of June.

sentence.da: Det er den **anden** dør til højre.
sentence.en: It is the second door on the right.

appelsinjuice.explanation: "Appelsinjuice" is orange juice, and it is an en-word. The word is built from "appelsin" (orange) and "juice" (juice), and written as one word. Ask for "et glas appelsinjuice" (a glass of orange juice) in a cafe. It is often on the breakfast table.

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have et glas **appelsinjuice**.
sentence.en: I would like a glass of orange juice.

april.explanation: "April" is April, written with a small letter. You say "i april" for in April. The weather in Denmark in April is famously unpredictable, and there is an old saying about "aprilsnar" (April fool), which is the Danish way to say "April fool!".

sentence.en: The weather is changeable in April.

arabisk.explanation: "Arabisk" means Arabic and is used both for the language and for things connected to the Arab world. It is written with a small letter and does not add -t before an et-word. Many people in Denmark speak Arabic at home, so it is a useful word to know.

sentence.en: She speaks both Danish and Arabic.

asien.explanation: "Asien" is the Danish name for Asia, written with a capital letter. Say "i Asien" for being there and "til Asien" for going there. A person from Asia is "en asiat", and the describing word is "asiatisk". It is the biggest of the continents.

sentence.en: We are going on holiday in Asia.

at arbejde.explanation: "At arbejde" means to work: "Jeg arbejder på et hospital" (I work at a hospital). It is used for jobs and for effort. "Arbejde" is also a word for work itself, as in "Jeg har meget arbejde" (I have a lot of work), and then it is an et-word. Remember the spelling with -ejd-, which is not spelled like it sounds.

sentence.en: I work in an office.

atten.explanation: Means "eighteen". It comes from "otte" (eight), but the spelling changes to "atten". The ending is shared with the other teens. In Denmark 18 is the age at which a person becomes an adult, so you may hear "atten år" often.

sentence.da: Hun er **atten** år og bor hjemme.
sentence.en: She is eighteen and lives at home.

august.explanation: "August" is August, written with a small letter, and you say "i august" for in August. It is the end of the summer holidays in Denmark, and school starts again around this time. The spelling is the same as in English, but with a small letter.

sentence.en: School starts again in August.

australien.explanation: "Australien" is the Danish name for Australia, with a capital letter. It ends in "-ien", like "Asien". Say "i Australien" for being there and "til Australien" for going there. A person from there is "en australier", and the describing word is "australsk".

sentence.en: My brother lives in Australia.

en adresse.explanation: "Adresse" is an address, like where someone lives. In Danish addresses the street name comes first and the number follows, for example "Vestergade 12", and the postcode comes before the town. The plural is "adresser".

sentence.en: What is your address?

en afgang.explanation: "Afgang" is a departure, for example of a train, bus or plane. You will see it on timetable boards at stations and airports, next to "ankomst" (arrival). For people leaving, Danes more often use the verb "at tage afsted" or "at rejse".

sentence.en: The departure is at nine o'clock.

en aftale.explanation: "En aftale" is an agreement or an appointment you have made. People say "Det er en aftale!" for "It's a deal!". "At have en aftale" means to have plans or an appointment, for example at the doctor's. The plural is "aftaler".

sentence.en: I have an appointment with the doctor.

en aften.explanation: En aften is an evening. In Danish, "the evening" is "aftenen". Useful phrases are "i aften" (this evening, tonight), "om aftenen" (in the evening, as a habit) and "god aften" (good evening). The meal people eat in the evening is "aftensmad" (evening food), so Danish builds on this word often.

sentence.en: We are eating together tonight.

en agurk.explanation: "En agurk" is a cucumber. It is a very common ingredient in Danish salads and on open sandwiches, and pickled cucumber ("asier" or "syltede agurker") is a classic topping on hot dogs. Be careful not to mix it up with "en salat", which is lettuce or a whole salad.

sentence.en: I am cutting a cucumber for the salad.

en albue.explanation: "En albue" is an elbow. The u is pronounced like a w sound, so it sounds like "al-boo-e". It is the joint in the middle of your arm, and a common injury phrase is "Jeg har slået albuen" (I have hit my elbow).

sentence.en: I hit my elbow on the table.

en alder.explanation: "Alder" is how old someone is, and it is almost always used in just one form. To ask someone's age in everyday speech Danes say "Hvor gammel er du?" (How old are you?) rather than using "alder"; "alder" sounds more formal, like on a form. You will also see it in set phrases such as "i min alder" (at my age).

sentence.en: What is your age?

en allergi.explanation: "En allergi" is an allergy. In a restaurant you can say "Jeg har en allergi" or be specific, for example "Jeg har en nøddeallergi" (a nut allergy). Pronounce the end like "-ee", and note that the plural is "allergier".

sentence.da: Jeg har en **allergi** over for nødder.
sentence.en: I have an allergy to nuts.

en ambulance.explanation: "En ambulance" is an ambulance. The emergency number in Denmark is 112, and you say "Ring efter en ambulance" (Call for an ambulance). The word is spoken a bit like the English one, with a French-style "ng" in the middle.

sentence.en: Call for an ambulance!

en amerikaner.explanation: "En amerikaner" is a person from the USA. Is used for both men and women. The plural is "amerikanere". The describing word is "amerikansk". Note that the Danish word is not capitalised, unlike English.

sentence.da: Hun er **amerikaner**, men bor i Danmark.
sentence.en: She is American but lives in Denmark.

en ananas.explanation: "En ananas" is a pineapple. And the word is the same as in many languages. The extra "s" appears in the forms: "ananassen" and "ananasser". Pineapple is a favourite on some pizzas, which Danes joke about.

sentence.en: I love fresh pineapple.

en and.explanation: "En and" is a duck. The plural is irregular: "ænder", with an "æ" instead of an "a". Be careful that "anden" means "the duck" but also "the other" or "second" (as in "den anden"), so the context matters. Feeding the ducks at a pond is a common activity with children.

sentence.en: The children are feeding the duck by the lake.

en ankomst.explanation: "Ankomst" is an arrival, the time or place where someone or something arrives. On boards in stations and airports it sits opposite "afgang" (departure). Look for the word on the screens to see when your train or plane comes in. The matching verb is "at ankomme".

sentence.en: The arrival is at twelve o'clock.

en app.explanation: "En app" is a small program on your phone or tablet, the same as in English. And the word "the" goes on the end: "appen". You will also hear "apps" for more than one, but "apper" is the Danish-style form. You "henter" (download) or "åbner" (open) an app.

sentence.en: I use the app every day.

en appelsin.explanation: "En appelsin" is the fruit orange. The word "orange" is also used in Danish for the colour, so the fruit and the colour have different words. Fresh orange juice is "appelsinjuice", which you will see on most breakfast tables and menus.

sentence.en: I peeled an orange for the children.

en arm.explanation: "En arm" is an arm. The word for more than one is "arme". Say "Hun har brækket armen" for "She has broken her arm". Remember that Danish uses "armen" (the arm) where English would say "her arm".

sentence.en: He has broken his arm.

en avis.explanation: "En avis" is a newspaper. The plural "aviser" adds -er. You read it with "at læse avisen", and a journalist is "en journalist". Many Danes now read the news online, and then "nyheder" (news) is a handy word too.

sentence.en: My dad reads the newspaper every morning.

et ansigt.explanation: "Et ansigt" is the face. Remember the g and the t are both pronounced softly, so it sounds a bit like "an-seet". Danes say "Vask dit ansigt" (Wash your face), and "et glad ansigt" would be "a happy face" in everyday talk.

sentence.en: She has a beautiful face.

et apotek.explanation: "Et apotek" is a pharmacy, where you buy medicine. In Denmark many medicines, even simple ones like painkillers, are sold only at the pharmacy, not in ordinary shops. The person working there is "en apoteker" or "en farmaceut".

sentence.da: Jeg skal på **apoteket** og købe medicin.
sentence.en: I need to go to the pharmacy and buy medicine.

et arbejde.explanation: "Et arbejde" is work or a job. It is used a lot: "Jeg er på arbejde" means "I am at work", and "at gå på arbejde" is to go to work. Use "et job" when you mean a specific position, and "arbejde" for work in general. The verb is "at arbejde".

sentence.en: I have to go to work now.
